name: Hypothesis Testing Common Pitfalls
description: This module lists the most common pitfalls encountered in hypothesis testing work, so they can be actively avoided rather than rediscovered.
content:
This module lists the most common pitfalls encountered in hypothesis testing work, so they can be actively avoided rather than rediscovered.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Document any non-obvious hypothesis testing decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
2. State assumptions about hypothesis testing explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
3. Before starting hypothesis testing work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
4. Measure before optimizing any hypothesis testing bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
5. When hypothesis testing guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
6. Prefer the simplest hypothesis testing approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
7. Keep hypothesis testing changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
8. Re-check edge cases relevant to hypothesis testing (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
9. When hypothesis testing decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
10. Keep hypothesis testing outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
11. When multiple hypothesis testing strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
12. Validate hypothesis testing outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Avoid introducing new hypothesis testing abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not silently drop hypothesis testing edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Do not apply generic hypothesis testing advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Avoid mixing unrelated hypothesis testing concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.
- Do not skip documenting hypothesis testing assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.

CLOSING NOTE
When in doubt, prefer clarity and explicit reasoning about hypothesis testing over a shortcut that saves a few lines but hides intent.
